subject: combined-science

items.q: A student follows the reaction between marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid, which gives off carbon dioxide. Which set of measurements would allow the mean rate of reaction to be worked out?
items.correct: The volume of gas collected, together with the time taken to collect it
items.misconception: The total volume of gas given off at the end, and nothing else
items.why: 'How much gas did it make?' and 'how fast did it make it?' both feel like measures of how well the reaction went. The rate of a chemical reaction is found by measuring the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of product formed over time. A quantity on its own is not a rate.
items.random_wrong: The time taken until the fizzing finally stops, and nothing more

items.q: In a reaction, 3.6 g of magnesium ribbon is used up in 180 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
items.misconception: 0.020 g/min
items.why: Practical work is often described in minutes while the readings are taken in seconds, so the two time units are swapped without converting. The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s. Changing the time unit changes the number as well, so the value and the unit must agree.
items.random_wrong: 50 g/s

items.q: A gas syringe collects 12 cm³ of gas in 8 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
items.correct: 1.5 cm³ /s
items.misconception: 0.67 cm³ /s
items.why: Students remember that a division is needed but not which way round, and dividing the big number by the small one gives a tidier answer. The quantity always goes on top: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken).
items.random_wrong: 1.5 cm³ /min

items.q: The specification states how the quantity of a reactant or product may be measured. Which pair does it give?
items.correct: The mass measured in grams or the volume in cm³
items.misconception: The concentration in mol/dm³ or the temperature in °C
items.why: Concentration and temperature are the quantities most often written on the bottles and read off in rate experiments, so they feel like the measured quantity. The quantity of reactant or product can be measured by the mass in grams or by a volume in cm³ . Temperature is a condition, not a quantity of substance.
items.random_wrong: The mass in grams or the total time taken in seconds

items.q: Which of these is given in the specification as a unit of rate of reaction?
items.correct: cm³ /s
items.misconception: s/cm³
items.why: The unit is assembled from the words in the order they were spoken ('seconds per centimetre cubed') rather than from the division that was done. The quantity divided by the time gives the quantity on top: g/s or cm³ /s, and mol/s at Higher Tier.
items.random_wrong: mol/dm³

items.q: (HT) In a Higher Tier question the quantity of a reactant is given in moles. In which unit should the rate of reaction then be given?
items.correct: mol/s
items.misconception: mol/dm³
items.why: mol/dm³ is the unit met most often with moles, in concentration work, so it is recalled first. For the Higher Tier, quantity of reactants may be in moles and units for rate of reaction in mol/s. mol/dm³ is a concentration, not a rate.
items.random_wrong: s /mol

items.q: (HT) In a reaction, 0.60 mol of hydrogen is produced in 30 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
items.correct: 0.020 mol/s
items.misconception: 0.020 mol/min
items.why: Practical work is often described in minutes while the readings are taken in seconds, so the two time units are swapped without converting. The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s. Changing the time unit changes the number as well, so the value and the unit must agree.

items.q: A flask of reacting mixture stands on a balance. The mass falls from 82.50 g to 81.90 g in 120 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
items.why: Practical work is often described in minutes while the readings are taken in seconds, so the two time units are swapped without converting. The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s. Changing the time unit changes the number as well, so the value and the unit must agree.

items.q: Experiment X produces 30 cm³ of gas in 20 s. Experiment Y produces 45 cm³ of gas in 45 s. Which statement about the mean rates is correct?
items.correct: X is faster: its mean rate is 1.5 cm³ /s and the mean rate of Y is 1.0 cm³ /s
items.misconception: Y is faster, because Y produces the larger total volume of gas
items.why: The bigger number of cm³ is the more obvious comparison, and the times are not brought into it. Rates must be compared after dividing each quantity by its own time taken.
items.random_wrong: Y is faster, because the reaction in Y was allowed to run for longer

items.q: A graph of the volume of gas produced against time is steep at first and then becomes less steep. What does this shape show?
items.correct: The reaction is fastest at the start, and then slows down
items.misconception: The volume of gas begins to fall once the curve bends over
items.why: A curve bending over is read as a curve going down, especially when it is described as 'levelling off'. The line still rises, just more slowly, so gas is still being made but at a lower rate.
items.random_wrong: The reaction speeds up steadily as more product forms

items.q: The line on a graph of volume of gas against time becomes horizontal after 80 s. What does this tell you?
items.correct: No more gas is being made, so the reaction has ended
items.misconception: Gas is now being made at a steady, constant rate
items.why: 'Straight line' is remembered as 'constant rate' from other graphs, without checking that this straight line has zero slope. A horizontal line has a gradient of zero, so the rate is zero and no more product is forming.
items.random_wrong: The reaction is still speeding up, but more gradually

items.q: A student needs the rate of reaction at 30 s from a curved graph of volume of gas against time. What should the student do?
items.correct: Draw a tangent at 30 s and work out its slope
items.misconception: Read the volume off the curve at 30 s and use that
items.why: The graph gives a value at 30 s easily, and a reading feels like an answer while a slope feels like extra work. The height of the curve is the quantity so far. The rate is the slope of the tangent at that point.
items.random_wrong: Join the origin to the point at 30 s and use that slope

items.q: (HT) A tangent drawn to a volume-time curve at 20 s passes through the points (10 s, 12 cm³ ) and (30 s, 52 cm³ ). What is the rate of reaction at 20 s?
items.correct: 2.0 cm³ /s
items.misconception: 0.50 cm³ /s
items.why: Students remember that a division is needed but not which way round, and dividing the big number by the small one gives a tidier answer. The quantity always goes on top: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of reactant used) / (time taken).
items.random_wrong: 40 cm³ /s

items.q: Which list contains only factors that the specification says affect the rate of a chemical reaction?
items.correct: Concentration, pressure of gases, surface area, temperature, catalysts
items.misconception: Concentration, pressure of gases, surface area, temperature, time
items.why: Longer experiments give more product, so time is confused with a factor that changes the rate itself. Time changes how much product has formed, not how fast it forms. The specification lists concentration, pressure of reacting gases, surface area, temperature and catalysts.
items.random_wrong: Concentration, colour of the reactants, temperature, stirring, catalysts

items.q: A reaction mixture is cooled from 40 °C to 20 °C. What happens to the rate of the reaction?
items.correct: It decreases, as collisions are less frequent and less energetic
items.misconception: It increases, because cooling packs the particles closer together
items.why: Cooling is linked to contraction and to particles slowing and settling, which is then read as particles being closer and so colliding more. Lowering the temperature lowers both the frequency and the energy of collisions, so the rate falls.
items.random_wrong: It is unchanged, since temperature affects only the final amount made

items.q: Required practical 5 investigates how changes in concentration affect the rate of reaction. Which pair of methods does the specification require?
items.correct: Measuring the volume of a gas, and following a colour change or turbidity
items.misconception: Measuring the volume of a gas, and following the temperature rise in the flask
items.why: Thermometers are used so often in practical chemistry that a temperature measurement is assumed to be part of any rate experiment. Required practical 5 uses a method involving measuring the volume of a gas produced and a method involving a change in colour or turbidity.
items.random_wrong: Measuring the temperature rise, and following a colour change or turbidity

items.q: Required practical 5 should involve developing a hypothesis. Which of these is a suitable hypothesis for the investigation?
items.correct: The higher the concentration of the acid, the faster gas will be produced
items.misconception: Measure the volume of gas every ten seconds for each concentration used
items.why: The method is the part of a write-up that is planned first and takes the most effort, so it is remembered as the important statement. A hypothesis is a testable prediction made before the results are collected; the steps are the method and the summary of the results is the conclusion.
items.random_wrong: Add the acid to the magnesium and time each reaction with a stopwatch

items.q: According to collision theory, when can a reaction between two particles take place?
items.correct: Only when they collide with at least the activation energy
items.misconception: Whenever they collide, no matter how gently they hit each other
items.why: Collision theory is remembered as 'particles must collide' and the energy condition attached to it is dropped. Chemical reactions can occur only when reacting particles collide with each other and with sufficient energy.
items.random_wrong: Only when the collision itself gives out enough energy

items.q: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?
items.correct: The minimum energy that particles must have in order to react
items.misconception: The energy given out as the products are formed
items.why: Energy changes in reactions are met as energy released, so any energy quantity in a reaction is assumed to be energy given out. Activation energy is the minimum amount of energy that particles must have to react. It is a requirement to be met, not an output.
items.random_wrong: The energy that is given out when the particles collide and react

items.q: Why does increasing the concentration of hydrochloric acid increase the rate of its reaction with magnesium?
items.correct: More particles in the same volume means more frequent collisions
items.misconception: The acid particles move faster, so their collisions carry more energy
items.why: 'Stronger' and 'more concentrated' get mixed with 'hotter', and faster particles are the explanation used for temperature. Increasing the concentration of reactants in solution increases the frequency of collisions. Particle speed depends on temperature, not concentration.
items.random_wrong: The activation energy of the reaction is lowered by the extra acid

items.q: A 5 g strip of magnesium and 5 g of magnesium powder are added to separate beakers of the same acid. Why does the powder react faster?
items.correct: It has a larger surface area to volume ratio, so collisions are more frequent
items.misconception: There is simply more magnesium in the powder than in the strip
items.why: The powder looks like more material because it spreads out, and equal masses are not compared. The masses are the same. Cutting a solid into smaller pieces increases its surface area to volume ratio, exposing more particles to collide.
items.random_wrong: The powder particles move faster, so the collisions are more energetic

items.q: Why does raising the temperature increase the rate of a reaction? Give the full reason.
items.correct: Collisions are more frequent and more of them are energetic enough
items.misconception: Collisions are more frequent, and that is the whole of the reason why
items.why: The collision-frequency explanation works for concentration and pressure, so it is reused for temperature and the energy half is left out. Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic, and so increases the rate of reaction.
items.random_wrong: Collisions happen more often, and nothing else about them changes

items.q: Two gases react together. Why does increasing the pressure of the gases increase the rate of reaction?
items.correct: The particles are in a smaller volume, so they collide more often
items.misconception: Squeezing the particles closer together makes each collision harder
items.why: Pressure is felt as a force pushing particles together, and a harder push sounds like a harder collision. Increasing the pressure of reacting gases increases the frequency of collisions. The energy of the collisions depends on temperature.
items.random_wrong: Raising the pressure lowers the energy that a successful collision needs

items.q: Doubling the concentration of a solution roughly doubles the rate of reaction. Using simple ideas about proportionality, what should halving the concentration do?
items.correct: Roughly halve the rate, as collisions become half as frequent
items.misconception: Cut the rate to a quarter, since the rate depends on the square
items.why: 'Proportional' is confused with a squared relationship, or the halving is applied twice. Simple proportionality is what the specification asks for: half the particles in the same volume gives about half the collision frequency and about half the rate.
items.random_wrong: Cut the rate by more than half, as the particles also move slower

items.q: Which statement about catalysts is correct?
items.correct: A catalyst changes the rate of a reaction but is not used up by it
items.misconception: A catalyst is used up slowly, so more must be added as it goes
items.why: Everything else added to a reaction mixture gets consumed, so a catalyst is assumed to behave the same way. A catalyst can be recovered at the end and is not included in the chemical equation for the reaction.
items.random_wrong: One catalyst will speed up any reaction that it is added to

items.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a chemical reaction?
items.correct: It provides a different pathway with a lower activation energy
items.misconception: It lowers the activation energy of the original reaction pathway
items.why: 'Lowers the activation energy' is the half of the sentence that gets remembered, and the different pathway is dropped. Catalysts increase the rate of reaction by providing a different pathway for the reaction that has a lower activation energy.
items.random_wrong: It speeds up any reaction at all, as catalysts always do

items.q: On a reaction profile for a catalysed reaction, how does the catalysed curve differ from the uncatalysed one?
items.correct: Its hump is lower, and the reactants and products are unchanged
items.misconception: Its hump is lower, and the products end up at a lower energy too
items.why: One lowered feature on the diagram is generalised to the whole curve being pulled down. A reaction profile for a catalysed reaction is drawn with a lower activation energy hump, while the reactant and product energies are unchanged.
items.random_wrong: Its hump is lower, and it makes more product as well

items.q: The equation for a reaction is 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. A solid is added to the flask, the reaction speeds up, and the solid is recovered unchanged at the end. What is the solid?
items.correct: A catalyst, as it speeds the reaction up and is not in the equation
items.misconception: A reactant, because it was added to the flask before the reaction started
items.why: Anything put into the flask at the beginning is assumed to be a reactant. Students should be able to identify catalysts in reactions from their effect on the rate of reaction and because they are not included in the chemical equation.
items.random_wrong: A product, because it was there in the flask at the end of the reaction

items.q: Reaction A finishes in 20 s, reaction B in 200 s, and both make the same amount of gas. Which has the greater rate?
items.correct: Reaction A: the same quantity of gas in a shorter time is a faster reaction.
items.misconception: Reaction B is faster because 200 is a bigger number of seconds than 20.
items.why: Time is the number the student actually measured, so it feels like the answer, and in everyday speech 'a long reaction' sounds like 'a big reaction'. Time is the denominator, not the rate. Mean rate of reaction = (quantity of product formed) / (time taken), so a longer time gives a smaller rate for the same quantity.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A rate is worked out as 0.6. How should it be written?
items.correct: 0.6 cm³ /s, because a rate is a quantity per second.
items.misconception: 0.6 cm³ , because that is the unit of the quantity that was measured.
items.why: The unit is copied from the measuring cylinder or balance and the 'per second' part of the calculation is forgotten. The units of rate of reaction may be given as g/s or cm³ /s: the time unit must appear.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: 0.060 mol of hydrogen forms in 30 s. What is the mean rate?
items.correct: 0.0020 mol/s, from 0.060 divided by 30.
items.misconception: 1.8 mol/s, from 0.060 multiplied by 30.
items.why: Multiplying is the safer-feeling operation when the numbers are awkward, and it avoids a small decimal answer. Rate is a division: mean rate of reaction = (quantity of product formed) / (time taken).
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A flask loses 0.60 g of mass in 120 s. What is the mean rate of reaction?
items.correct: 0.0050 g/s, from 0.60 g divided by 120 s.
items.misconception: 0.60 g/s, because 0.60 g is what the reaction lost.
items.why: The mass loss is the number the student worked out first, so it is reported as the answer with a rate unit stuck on the end. The mass lost is the quantity of reactant used. It must still be divided by the time taken to give a rate.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A student joins the origin to the point at 30 s and calls the slope the rate at 30 s. Is that right?
items.correct: No: that gives the mean rate over the first 30 s, not the rate at 30 s.
items.misconception: The line from the origin to the point gives the rate at that moment.
items.why: Both lines are straight and both have a slope, so the difference between an average over a period and a value at an instant is missed. A tangent touches the curve at the point and matches its steepness there, which is why the specification asks for a tangent.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A tangent rises 40 cm³ while time goes from 10 s to 30 s. What is the rate?
items.correct: 2.0 cm³ /s, from 40 cm³ divided by 20 s.
items.misconception: 40 cm³ /s, using the rise on its own.
items.why: The vertical change is the number that stands out on the graph, and the horizontal change is not read off. The gradient of a tangent is the change in quantity divided by the change in time.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does changing the temperature change the rate of a reaction, or only the amount of product?
items.correct: It changes the rate: higher temperature means a faster reaction.
items.misconception: Temperature only affects how much product is made, not how quickly.
items.why: Yield and rate are both described as 'how well the reaction went', and the two are not separated. Students should be able to recall how changing temperature affects the rate of chemical reactions: raising it increases the rate.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does raising the concentration, pressure or surface area change the activation energy?
items.correct: No: it changes how often particles collide, not the energy they need.
items.misconception: These changes lower the activation energy of the reaction.
items.why: Activation energy is the phrase most firmly attached to rate, so it is offered as the explanation for every change that speeds a reaction up. Only a catalyst provides a pathway with a lower activation energy. The other factors work by changing collision frequency, or frequency and energy for temperature.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Will one good catalyst speed up any reaction?
items.correct: No: different reactions need different catalysts.
items.misconception: A catalyst is a general speeding-up substance that works on any reaction.
items.why: The word catalyst is used loosely outside chemistry to mean anything that makes something happen faster. Different reactions need different catalysts, and enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does adding a catalyst increase the amount of product a reaction makes?
items.correct: No: it changes the rate, so the same product is made sooner.
items.misconception: A catalyst makes the reaction produce more product than it would otherwise.
items.why: Faster and more are both improvements, so they are treated as the same improvement. A catalyst changes the rate of the reaction. The reactants and products, and their energies on a reaction profile, are unchanged.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are enzymes catalysts?
items.correct: Yes: enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems.
items.misconception: Any solid substance that speeds up a reaction must be an enzyme.
items.why: Enzymes are met in biology and catalysts in chemistry, so the two are filed separately. Enzymes act as catalysts in biological systems, speeding reactions up without being used up.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is stirring one of the factors the specification lists as affecting rate?
items.correct: No: the listed factors are concentration, pressure of reacting gases, surface area, temperature and catalysts.
items.misconception: Stirring the mixture, and the colour of the reactants, are factors that change the rate.
items.why: Stirring is something students always do in the laboratory and it does help mix reactants, so it is remembered as one of the taught factors; colour is confused with the colour change used to follow some reactions. The specification lists the concentrations of reactants in solution, the pressure of reacting gases, the surface area of solid reactants, the temperature and the presence of catalysts.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
